• Name: Babylonian snail
  • Scientific name: Babylonia spirata
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.021–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: carnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful (with caution)
  • Life span: up to 4–5 years
  • Colour: white to yellowish, with large orange to brown markings

Babylonia spirata grows quite large and prefers warm water. It is a carnivorous, opportunistic scavenger and is difficult, though possible, to breed in captivity.

Babylonia spirata is a relatively large species. The average shell is 4.5–5.5 cm in diameter and 25–35 g in weight.

Notable features include:

  • The shells are typically white to yellowish, with large orange to brown markings.
  • The shell is smooth, broad and ovoid with regular spiral rows.
  • Full-grown snails have 6 whorls.
  • The whorls are rather inflated and have deep sutures with a sharp edge.
  • The columella is smooth.
  • The aperture is large, ovate and constricted posteriorly.

It also has an operculum (the trap-door), which it uses to close its shell completely when disturbed or stressed. It also has a proboscis/siphon (mouth) that looks like an elephant's trunk and is also used for breathing and smelling.

In some cases it can be very difficult to distinguish Babylonia spirata from Babylonia zeylanica, as they look almost identical. However, Babylonia zeylanica grows a little bigger (up to 7.5 cm), its shell has slightly impressed sutures compared to Babylonia spirata, and it is distributed mostly in Indian and Sri Lankan waters.

Babylonia spirata grows fast and reaches its maximum size within 2–3 years. In aquariums, if appropriately cared for, it can live for 4–5 years.

The species is relatively sensitive to transportation stress. It is extremely important to transport the snails at least in a moist condition, covered with a wet jute bag or wet cotton soaked in seawater.

Babylonia spirata is widely distributed in the Indo-Pacific region, especially from the Western Indian Ocean to Bali, Indonesia. In India, these snails have been recorded from the southeast and southwest coasts and in waters around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Generally, they can be found at depths of 5–30 m in marine coastal waters, in silt or sandy benthic zones.

Babylonia spirata requires an established tank of sufficient size and water volume. The minimum recommended tank size for one large snail is 60 litres. The bigger the tank, the better. According to a study, different stocking densities affect the growth rate of the snails.

Another big problem with small tanks is that water parameters can be very difficult to keep stable. Unless you are already an expert, it is best to stay away from small setups.

Babylonia spirata is not difficult to care for, although the snails have some specific requirements if you want to create an ideal environment for them. Stable water parameters are important, so an established tank is needed (see Aquarium size and Water conditions).

Temperature: the preferred water temperature is 26–30°C, which is considered optimal. The species tolerates neither too low nor too high temperatures. Temperature is one of the most important physical factors influencing snails. It affects the survival rate, hatch rate, incubation period, larval feeding behaviour, larval growth, etc. According to a study:

  • At 20°C they close the operculum tightly.
  • If the temperature falls below 24°C, Babylonia spirata becomes inactive and lies above the substrate.
  • At 26°C the snails become a little more active and start responding slowly to food.
  • At 28°C Babylonia spirata shows normal movement, feeding and burrowing.
  • At 34°C the snails become inactive again. They cannot even fully retract into the shell.

pH: maintain pH at 8.1–8.4 for the snails to thrive in a saltwater aquarium.

Hardness: keep carbonate hardness at 8–12 dKH.

SG: specific gravity should be between 1.023 (30 ppt) and 1.025 (33 ppt). Juvenile and adult Babylonia spirata have been studied: normal activity and survival were observed at salinities of 27–35 ppt for juveniles and 31–35 ppt for adults. Salinities below 1.015 (19 ppt) were lethal, and all snails died after 24 hours of exposure.

Dissolved oxygen: 5–7 mg/L.

Nitrate should stay below 20 ppm.

Substrate: substrate plays a very important role in a snail's life. It provides attachment, shelter and nourishment, which are fundamental needs. The substrate should at least allow Babylonia spirata to bury itself.

Experiments with 4 types of substrate (gravel 1–2 mm, coarse sand 1.00–0.50 mm, fine sand 0.25–0.10 mm and silt 0.05–0.002 mm) showed a clear preference for silt (45.2 to 64.7%), followed by fine sand (16.8 and 31.7%). There was a negative correlation with gravel and coarse sand. Silt (preferably) and fine sand are therefore the best choices.

Lighting: although Babylonia spirata is nocturnal, studies have shown that photoperiod plays an important role in regulating its reproductive cycle. It has no strict lighting requirements, so lighting can be adapted to the needs of fish, corals, sea anemones, etc.

Acclimation: before putting the snails into the tank, acclimate them carefully, as with all invertebrates. Do it very slowly; in general 2–3 hours is enough.

Babylonia spirata is a scavenging gastropod mollusc that feeds mainly on dead and decayed animal matter present in the substrate where it lives. Scavenging snails are acutely sensitive to chemical messages emanating from food.

In the scientific literature there are some minor contradictions regarding the optimal diet. According to one study, the best results were obtained with a diet containing 40% dietary protein, compared with 30% and 35% protein diets. Another study showed that a 35% protein diet gave better results. In any case, the snail depends heavily on protein- and calcium-rich diets.

Protein deficiency can hinder growth and lead to weight loss, because protein is important for maintaining vital organs. Calcium is needed for several vital life processes in snails, the most obvious being the formation of the shell. Calcium carbonate is the basic natural compound of their shells.

In the aquarium, they eat leftover food, detritus, etc. However, if there are many snails or not enough leftovers and naturally occurring food, they can attack other snails. It is therefore better to supplement their diet with meaty foods, such as:

  • frozen brine and mysis shrimp,
  • freeze-dried larvae,
  • cut-up pieces of fish and seafood.

Experiments showed that, given a choice, they mostly prefer the meat of bivalves such as oysters, clams and mussels, or crustaceans such as prawns. Pellet food is the least preferred.

Laboratory observations of Babylonia spirata:

  • Snails may consume around 3–5% of their body weight in food.
  • Large snails (more than 5 cm) can consume up to 2 g of meat in 7 minutes.
  • They are acutely sensitive to chemical messages emanating from organic food.
  • The time taken to reach food placed 100 cm away ranged from 10 to 11 minutes.
  • Diet type: carnivore
  • Feeding frequency: 1–2 times a week

Babylonia spirata can be shy and quiet, especially when newly introduced into an aquarium. It is predominantly nocturnal and often buries itself in the substrate during the day. When hungry, however, it is relatively active at any time.

When buried, it extends the proboscis to the surface of the substrate like a periscope, which lets it smell dead organic matter while resting. It then quickly emerges from the substrate and moves toward the food.

According to studies, Babylonia snails have a complex olfactory system. Food can be detected from a distance of a few metres. Generally, they come out of the substrate within 5–10 minutes when food is placed anywhere in the tank.

Although carnivorous, they are not active predators and prefer dead animal matter. They are fairly lazy and do not move much. From time to time they may climb to the top of the tank, but this does not happen often. The foot is very long and strong, so when needed they can easily flip themselves upright.

  • Social: no
  • Active: no
  • Burrower: yes
  • Temperament: peaceful (with caution)

Reef safety: yes, they are reef safe. Babylonia spirata will not deliberately damage anything in a reef tank and will not try to snack on corals when looking for food. However, because of their size and strength they tend to knock things around and can simply bulldoze through corals. To prevent incidents, it is advised to glue corals to the rocks.

Tankmates: Babylonia spirata is not an aggressive species and is compatible with most tankmates. Nonetheless, if sufficient food is not provided, it may prey on other (smaller) snails. In general they are predatory whelks that eat animals located in the sand. However, full-grown snails (fighting conch, Cerith snails, Astrea snails, Mexican turbo snails, Trochus snails, etc.) should be relatively safe in any case. They are compatible with shrimp such as Sexy shrimp, Red Fire shrimp (Lysmata debelius), Peppermint shrimp (Lysmata wurdemanni) or Skunk Cleaner (Lysmata amboinensis).

Bad tankmates:

  • Large and/or aggressive fish
  • Aggressive shrimp (such as Coral banded shrimp)
  • Most crab species
  • All hermit crab species (including Halloween hermit crab, Blue Leg hermit crab, etc.)

Hermit crabs can try to kill the snails just for their shells. If you still decide to keep them together, make sure the hermit crabs have numerous empty shells spread out through the tank. However, this can only reduce aggression, not eliminate it.

Babylonia spirata is not a hermaphrodite. Males and females can be distinguished by external features.

  • Size: at the same age, females are a little larger and heavier than males.
  • Reproductive organs: males can be identified externally by a male organ on the right side of the head, just behind the right tentacle. Females have a pedal gland on the ventral side of the foot, which shapes and hardens the egg capsule.

The pet industry mostly depends on wild-caught animals, even though the breeding process of this species is fully described in scientific literature. Babylonia spirata can breed in home aquariums as well; the main problem is the survival of the larvae because of their specific diet requirements.

Mating

Males usually mature at a size of 3.6 cm, while females mature at 3.9 cm. The smallest recorded mature female was 3.1 cm and the smallest male was 2.8 cm long.

The process starts with the female positioning herself on the right side of the male and mounting slightly over him. It lasts 2–3 hours, during which the snails remain immobile. Afterwards the male moves away first, leaving the female inactive for some time.

Mating does not depend on the time of day; it was observed during both day and night. During the spawning period, females do not eat even if food is placed near them.

Fertilization

Babylonia spirata is gonochoristic with internal fertilization.

Eggs

After fertilization, females deposit egg capsules. It takes 5–10 minutes to release a single capsule. The average number of capsules is 35 to 40, with 350–800 eggs per capsule, so each snail may potentially produce 12,000 to 32,000 eggs.

The jelly-like capsules harden on contact with seawater. Females firmly attach the transparent egg capsules to the substrate to hold them upright until the larvae hatch.

Larvae

Babylonia spirata has indirect development, with an initial capsular phase followed by a planktonic phase (veligers or larvae). Hatching happens on the 7th and 8th days after spawning. After hatching, the larvae immediately swim to the water surface using fast-moving cilia. The larvae exhibit phototaxis, the ability to move directionally in response to a light source.

During the next 10 days, the larvae feed on phytoplankton. In laboratory experiments, higher survival (around 3%) was observed in veliger larvae fed a mixed culture of Isochrysis and Chaetoceros, or I. galbana and C. calcifrans, at a density of 20,000 cells/cc twice daily. After that they can also be given Tetraselmis. Poor growth and heavy larval mortality occurred when they were fed T. gracilis and N. salina.

Metamorphosis from larva to juvenile occurs when the shell length reaches 1.7 mm and the weight is around 0.01 g. After settlement, the planktonic life ends and the snails become carnivores.

Scientists noticed that after reaching the juvenile stage, at a shell length of less than 5 mm, Babylonia spirata does something strange: the little snails crawl up the tank wall, cannot get back into the water and die soon afterwards.

At the crawling juvenile stage, the snails can be fed:

  • early hatched frozen artemia (for 2 weeks),
  • adult frozen artemia (subsequently),
  • artificial shrimp feed,
  • agar-based feed,
  • egg yolk,
  • egg albumin,
  • tubifex worms,
  • rotifers, etc.

After 4–5 weeks, they can start eating small pieces of fish meat once daily.

Rearing tank

The rearing tanks should have the same water parameters, at a density of 150 larvae/l. Before adding the larvae, it is recommended to treat the water with a hypochlorite and potassium permanganate solution to eliminate unwanted microorganisms.

Aeration also influences the hatching process of the larvae. In the experimental tank with aeration, the larvae swam actively in the water column, while in the treatment without aeration they usually stayed at the bottom of the tank.

These snails are traditionally exploited for the shell-craft industries. Babylonia spirata meat is also a valuable food with high-quality protein and a well-balanced diet enriched with essential vitamins and minerals; its nutritional content is protein (53.86%), carbohydrate (16.85%) and lipid (9.30%). The operculum is exported to foreign countries for manufacturing medicine and perfumes.

Babylonia spirata belongs to a diverse group of carnivorous whelks that are scavengers and predators. Although not very aggressive, its behaviour can change depending on food availability. Caring for it is not difficult and can be recommended even for beginners; just keep in mind that the species requires very warm temperatures.
